Single-layer framework of variational tensor network states

Hongyu Chen Address: School of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China    Yangfeng Fu Address: School of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China    Weiqiang Yu Address: School of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China    Rong Yu Address: School of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China    Z. Y. Xie Email: qingtaoxie@ruc.edu.cn Address: School of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China
Abstract

We propose a single-layer tensor network framework for the variational determination of ground states in two-dimensional quantum lattice models. By combining the nested tensor network method [Phys. Rev. B 96, 045128 (2017)] with the automatic differentiation technique, our approach can reduce the computational cost by three orders of magnitude in bond dimension, and therefore enables highly efficient variational ground-state calculations. We demonstrate the capability of this framework through two quantum spin models: the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model on a square lattice and the frustrated Shastry-Sutherland model. Even without GPU acceleration or symmetry implementation, we have achieved a bond dimension of nine and obtained accurate ground-state energy and consistent order parameters compared to prior studies. In particular, we confirm the existence of an intermediate empty-plaquette valence bond solid ground state in the Shastry-Sutherland model. We have further discussed the convergence of the algorithm and its potential improvements. Our work provides a promising route for large-scale tensor network calculations of two-dimensional quantum systems.

I Introduction

Two-dimensional (2D) strongly correlated systems, such as interacting fermionic systems and frustrated quantum magnets, pose significant challenges for theoretical studies. Consequently, developing efficient and accurate numerical methods for these models constitutes a crucial branch of theoretical condensed matter physics. In recent decades, tensor network methods [1, 2] have attracted increasing attention. By combining the tensor-network ansatz [3, 4] stemming from the quantum entanglement, the contraction strategy originating from renormalization group [6, 5], and modern optimization techniques developed in artificial intelligence [7], tensor network methods have been successfully applied to diverse phenomena, including quantum magnetism [8, 9, 10, 11], superconductivity [12, 13, 14], topological order [15, 16], and quantum field theory [17, 18].

For studying ground states of 2D quantum systems using tensor networks, three strategies are commonly adopted. The first maps the 2D quantum model to a three-dimensional classical one [19], converting the quantum expectation value calculation into a statistical physics problem [20]. The second employs imaginary-time evolution with wave function update schemes [21, 22, 23, 24] to obtain the ground state |Ψg⟩|\Psi_{g}\rangle in the tensor-network representation, and then evaluate the expectation value ⟨O^⟩\langle\hat{O}\rangle of the operator O^\hat{O} by contracting the related tensor networks. The third one is the straightforward variational minimization: Starting from an arbitrary tensor network state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle, the ground state of the system |Ψg⟩|\Psi_{g}\rangle and its energy EgE_{g} are obtained by minimizing the energy estimator

E=⟨Ψ|H^|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\displaystyle E=\frac{\langle\Psi|\hat{H}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle} (1)

with respect to tensor parameters [3]. Recently, this approach has become increasingly popular because of the advent of the automatic differentiation technique [25], which, as a mature and widely applied algorithm [26], can efficiently calculate the gradient d​Ed​|Ψ⟩\frac{dE}{d|\Psi\rangle} [27] and easily integrate with gradient-based optimization method [7] via various open-source packages [28, 29].

A central challenge in all three approaches is the contraction of tensor networks. Unfortunately, contracting a general tensor network in more than one dimension is a #​P\#P-complete hard problem [30] that cannot be performed exactly for an infinite system even with translational invariance. To this end, a series of approximation algorithms based on the renormalization group idea have been developed [5, 1], among which the corner transfer-matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) [31, 32, 14, 33] has been widely used. In two dimensions, the cost of the CTMRG algorithm scales as D10D^{10} in memory and D12D^{12} in computation with the bond dimension DD when no symmetry or partial matrix decomposition is employed. The cost is extremely high for variational calculations, which typically require hundreds of rounds of such contractions. The problem becomes even more serious for minimization with the automatic differentiation since it needs huge memory to store intermediate data for the gradient (d​Ed​|Ψ⟩\frac{dE}{d|\Psi\rangle}) calculation. This issue pose severe limitation for the bond dimension DD in variational minimization employing automatic differentiation.

To overcome this limitation, here we propose a single-layer framework of variational tensor network state calculation that incorporates the nested tensor network (NTN) method [34]. By reformulating the double-layer structures of numerator and denominator in Eq. (1) into nested single-layer structures, the NTN method reduces the memory and computation cost of tensor network contraction by two and three orders of DD, respectively. This allows us to perform variational minimization with significantly larger bond dimension. Our proposal works as follows: For any given state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle, we utilize the NTN to calculate the energy defined in Eq. (1), then calculate the gradient d​Ed​|Ψ⟩\frac{dE}{d|\Psi\rangle}, and finally update the wave function |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle using the gradient information as usual [27]. This procedure can be iterated many times until the calculated energy converges.

We validate this method on two benchmark models defined on infinite 2D lattices: the S=1/2S=1/2 square-lattice antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model and the frustrated Shastry-Sutherland model. The former has a long-range antiferromagnetically ordered ground state [35], while the latter hosts a series of ground states when tuning the strength of spin frustration J/J′J/J^{\prime} [36, 10]. In both cases, with the help of NTN, we can efficiently reach D=9D=9 even without any GPU utilization or symmetry implementation, which is difficult in previous variational calculations [27, 10, 11]. The obtained ground-state energy and order parameters are consistent with previous calculations, but with better convergence. In particular, we provide clear evidence for an empty-plaquette valence bond solid (VBS) phase in the ground-state phase diagram of the Shastry-Sutherland model.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II we first briefly review the automatic differentiation-assisted variational calculation of tensor network state and the NTN method, then introduce our single-layer framework. In Sec. III, we present the numerical results of the Heisenberg model and the Shastry-Sutherland model in detail. Finally, we summarize and conclude in Sec. IV.

II Method

In this section, we first review the basics of automatic differentiation-assisted variational calculation of tensor network representation of the ground state [27], the underlying double-layer structure in Eq. (1), and the NTN method [34], then introduce the single-layer framework by combining the two parts together.

II.1 Variational calculation assisted by automatic differentiation

For concreteness, we take the projected entangled pair state (PEPS) on a square lattice as an example to explain how to determine the ground state of a quantum spin system in the PEPS representation. Without loss of generality, suppose we have an infinite system hosting a 2×22\times 2 sublattice structure, then the infinite PEPS ansatz can be written as

|Ψ⟩=\displaystyle|\Psi\rangle= ∑{σ}[Tr∏iAr1​i​xi​c1​i​zi(i)[σi​a]Bxi​r3​i​c2​i​wi(i)[σi​b]\displaystyle\sum_{\{\sigma\}}\Big[\mathrm{Tr}\prod_{i}A^{(i)}_{r_{1i}x_{i}c_{1i}z_{i}}[\sigma_{ia}]B^{(i)}_{x_{i}r_{3i}c_{2i}w_{i}}[\sigma_{ib}]
Cr2​i​yi​zi​c3​i(i)[σi​c]Fyi​r4​i​wi​c4​i(i)[σi​f]]|…σi​aσi​bσi​cσi​f…⟩\displaystyle C^{(i)}_{r_{2i}y_{i}z_{i}c_{3i}}[\sigma_{ic}]F^{(i)}_{y_{i}r_{4i}w_{i}c_{4i}}[\sigma_{if}]\Big]\Big|\penalty\ ...\sigma_{ia}\sigma_{ib}\sigma_{ic}\sigma_{if}...\Big\rangle

where the superscript ii denotes the unit cell index, and A(i)A^{(i)}, B(i)B^{(i)}, C(i)C^{(i)}, F(i)F^{(i)} are the four distinct tensors defined in the ii-th unit cell. Tr means summing over all the tensor subscripts that correspond to the link indices, and ∑\sum means summation over all the physical spin configurations {σ}\{\sigma\}. A sketch of the |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle is illustrated in Fig. 1.

According to Eq. (), any quantum state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle satisfying the area law can be compatibly expressed as a superposition of spin configurations, where the coefficient of each term is represented as a tensor-network summation denoted by Tr. For an infinite system with translational symmetry, we assume the local tensors in different unit cells are the same, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). Therefore, for any given local tensors, we can introduce a shorthand

X=[A→,B→,C→,F→]\displaystyle X=[\vec{A},\vec{B},\vec{C},\vec{F}] (3)

where A→\vec{A} is the local tensor AA reshaped as a vector residing in the (D4​d)(D^{4}d)-dimensional space, and so are B→\vec{B}, C→\vec{C} and F→\vec{F}. X is then a (4​D4​d)(4D^{4}d)-dimensional vector storing all the variational parameters necessary to specify a quantum state |Ψ⁡(X)⟩|\Psi(X)\rangle represented as Eq. (). Here DD is the bond dimension, which is the upper bound of all the subscripts appeared in Eq. (), and dd is the physical dimension for each σ\sigma. A tensor with a larger DD contains more parameters, and is expected to have stronger representation power and better accuracy for a state. However, this also means heavier cost (discussed in Sec. II.2). To find the PEPS representation of the ground state |Ψg⟩|\Psi_{g}\rangle of a Hamiltonian system, we need to solve the following optimization problem

arg​minX​E​(X)\displaystyle\mathrm{arg\penalty\ min}_{X}E(X) (4)

where E⁡(X)E(X) is determined by Eq. (1) but now its dependence of XX is explicitly written.

In this work, we follow the variational minimization approach outlined in Sec. I. Starting from an initial |Ψ⁡(X0)⟩|\Psi(X_{0})\rangle, we can use well-established techniques, such as the CTMRG [31, 32, 14, 33], to compute the energy E⁡(X)E(X). In this procedure, when the automatic differentiation technique is used. Then, as long as EE is obtained successfully, we can calculate the gradient ∂E⁡(X)∂X|X=X0\frac{\partial{E(X)}}{\partial{X}}\big|_{X=X_{0}} conveniently by simply calling some open source packages, such as PyTorch [28] and Zygote [29], without any extra operation. After the gradient information is obtained, we can update XX using classic optimization algorithms, such as L-BFGS [7], to get a better trial X1X_{1} and the corresponding wave function |Ψ⁡(X1)⟩|\Psi(X_{1})\rangle. Similary, we can evaluate E⁡(X1)E(X_{1}), calculate ∂E⁡(X)∂X|X=X1\frac{\partial{E(X)}}{\partial{X}}\big|_{X=X_{1}}, and then obtain a better X2X_{2} and |Ψ⁡(X2)⟩|\Psi(X_{2})\rangle. This iteration can be repeated as many as we want until the gradient ∂E⁡(X)∂X\frac{\partial{E(X)}}{\partial{X}} is sufficiently small or the energy EE converges within some tolerance. The converged X∗X^{*} yields an approximate solution of Eq. (4) and thereby provides an approximate representation of |Ψg⟩|\Psi_{g}\rangle.

In essence, the reverse mode of automatic differentiation [25] uses the chain rule of derivative, usually referred to as backpropagation [37] in optimization engineering, to compute the gradient information. Formally, in this case

∂E∂X=∂E∂T(n)​∂T(n)∂T(n−1)​∂T(n−1)∂T(n−2)​…​∂T(2)∂T(1)​∂T(1)∂X\displaystyle\frac{\partial{E}}{\partial{X}}=\frac{\partial{E}}{\partial{T^{(n)}}}\frac{\partial{T^{(n)}}}{\partial{T^{(n-1)}}}\frac{\partial{T^{(n-1)}}}{\partial{T^{(n-2)}}}...\frac{\partial{T^{(2)}}}{\partial{T^{(1)}}}\frac{\partial{T^{(1)}}}{\partial{X}} (5)

where the {T(i),i=1,2,…​n}\{T^{(i)},i=1,2,...n\} are the intermediate variables that are involved in the process of evaluating EE, e.g., the temporary local tensors generated in the CTMRG iterations. We assume that nn related local tensors in Eq. (5) have been generated. In order to compute the gradient ∂E∂X\frac{\partial{E}}{\partial{X}}, these intermediate tensors generally need to be stored in memory. In the tensor network framework, if the transformations involved in the energy-evaluation contraction algorithms are treated as independent parameters, automatic differentiation is then equivalent to the backward iteration procedure of the second renormalization group method [38] for obtaining the global environment. Therefore, in this sense, this kind of variational tensor network approach tries to solve Eq. (4) by global optimization, and that is one of the reasons why this method can be successfully applied to study a series of strongly correlated systems [27], e.g., quantum spin-orbital liquid [39], altermagnetism [11], deconfined quantum critical point [10], even with a small bond dimension.

II.2 Review of the NTN method

As mentioned in the last section, the intermediate local tensors {T(i)}\{T^{(i)}\} in Eq. (5) have to be stored in memory before the gradient is obtained. This poses a great challenge for memory and strongly limits the bond dimension DD in the calculations. To see this, in Fig. 2, we sketch ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle whose calculation cannot be avoided in evaluating Eq. (1). Conventionally, to calculate ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle, firstly one need to form a reduced tensor

Ti​i′,j​j′,k​k′,l​l′a≡∑σAi,j,k,l​[σ]​Ai′,j′,k′,l′∗​[σ]\displaystyle T^{a}_{ii^{\prime},jj^{\prime},kk^{\prime},ll^{\prime}}\equiv\sum_{\sigma}A_{i,j,k,l}[\sigma]A^{*}_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime},l^{\prime}}[\sigma] (6)

as illustrated in Fig. 2(a). TbT^{b}, TcT^{c}, TfT^{f} can be defined similarly corresponding to the 2×22\times 2 unit cell in Fig. 1(a). Obviously, each local tensor TT, and thus the resulting tensor network ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle, has a double-layer structure. That is, if the representation |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle in Eq. () has bond dimension DD, then each index of TaT^{a} in Eq. (6) and the resulting ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle have bond dimension D2D^{2}. Therefore, evaluating the energy E⁡(X)E(X) requires contracting a tensor network with bond dimension D2D^{2}, which generally leads to a computational cost of about D12D^{12} [34] when the CTMRG algorithm is employed [40, 41]. As explained in Sec. II.1, the memory cost of storing all intermediate tensors generated in this procedure in automatic differentiation is typically D8D^{8}, which would expand fast with increasing DD. Therefore, the substantial memory and computational demands impose a stringent constraint on the practically attainable bond dimension DD in automatic differentiation-based variational minimization.

In order to solve this problem, the NTN method regards ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle as a single-layer network with a nesting structure, as illustrated in Fig. 2(c). To be specific, instead of summing over the physical index σ\sigma and forming a reduced tensor TaT^{a}, as done in Eq. (6), NTN considers the physical indices {σ}\{\sigma\} and the link indices equally by regarding {σ}\{\sigma\} as special link indices connecting nearby conjugated tensors, e.g, A∗A^{*} in ⟨Ψ|\langle\Psi| and AA in |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle, as shown in Fig. 2(b). In graphic terms, the bra state ⟨Ψ|\langle\Psi| (blue) and the ket state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle (red) lie in the same layer and are connected by {σ}\{\sigma\}. In order to avoid longer-range links, a virtual tensor XX, equal to the direct product of two δ\delta functions, is defined at each crossing point where the virtual links in ⟨Ψ|\langle\Psi| and |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle intersect. Furthermore, to make the resulting network a square lattice, we modify one set of XX to YY by combining an XX and a σ\sigma. Formally, as shown in Fig. 2(d), XX and YY can be defined as follows

Xi,j,k,l=δi​j​δk​l,Yi​σ,j,k,l​σ′=δi​j​δk​l​δσ​σ′\displaystyle X_{i,j,k,l}=\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl},\quad Y_{i\sigma,j,k,l\sigma^{\prime}}=\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\delta_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}} (7)

where δ\delta is the Kronecker-delta function. Finally, the nesting structure of ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle is illustrated in Fig. 2(c) as a single-layer network. Any expectation value of a local operator, such as local terms in the numerator in Eq. (1), i.e., ⟨Ψ|Hi​j|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|H_{ij}|\Psi\rangle where Hi​jH_{ij} is a bond Hamiltonian, can be represented similarly but with some impurity tensors.

Though the idea is simple, the NTN method has a significant advantage that the bond dimension of ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle is no more than D​dDd, where dd is the physical dimension associated with each σ\sigma, instead of D2D^{2} as in Fig. 2(a). Since the nesting structure is essentially a single-layer tensor network, widely used methods such as CTMRG can be employed to perform the contraction efficiently. For example, suppose the environment dimension used in CTMRG is of the same order as D2D^{2} required by the reduced tensor network with bond dimension D2D^{2}. In that case, ignoring the scaling of dd, the contraction of this nested single-layer tensor network has a memory cost of about D6D^{6} and a computational cost of about D9D^{9}, which are much lower than those in the reduced method (D8D^{8} and D12D^{12}) [34].

Bearing this advantage, the NTN method has been used in a series of studies to extend DD to larger values on the kagome lattice. For example, DD was extended to 2525 in Refs. [34, 8] to study the kagome spin liquid, also to 2525 in Ref. [40] to study the kagome Heisenberg model with DM interactions, and to 1515 in Ref. [41] to study the kagome Heisenberg model with chiral interactions.

II.3 The single-layer framework of variational tensor network states

As far as we know, in previous studies, such as Refs. [34, 8, 40, 41] mentioned in Sec. II.2, the NTN method was only utilized in either expectation value calculation or updating the wave function in imaginary-time evolution, but was seldom utilized in the variational calculation of the ground state wave function as discussed in Sec. II.1.

In this work, we propose to incorporate the NTN method into the variational solution of the minimization problem, i.e., Eq. (4). The overall framework is summarized in the following:

(i). First, we need to prepare an initial PEPS |Ψ⁡(X0)⟩|\Psi(X_{0})\rangle from which the optimization begins. Either an arbitrary state specified by a random X0X_{0} (this work) or an approximate PEPS obtained by imaginary-time evolution [21, 22, 23, 24] can be accepted.

(ii). Compute the energy E⁡(X0)E(X_{0}) through Eq. (1). where either boundary matrix product state [42, 43] or CTMRG (this work) can be used to contract the single-layer tensor network ⟨Ψ⁡(X0)|Ψ⁡(X0)⟩\langle\Psi(X_{0})|\Psi(X_{0})\rangle with nested structure explained in Sec. II.2. In this step, one can use automatic differentiation software packages, such as PyTorch [28] and Zygote [29] (this work), to implement the contraction algorithm. Once E⁡(X0)E(X_{0}) is obtained, the gradient ∂E⁡(X)∂X|X=X0\frac{\partial E(X)}{\partial X}\big|_{X=X_{0}} can be evaluated through Eq. (5) efficiently and automatically.

(iii). Using the gradient information obtained in step (ii), we can employ gradient-based optimization algorithm, such as Adam and L-BFGS [7] (this work), to get X1X_{1}, the updated estimate of the solution of Eq. (4). Then update the parameter by setting X0=X1X_{0}=X_{1} and obtain a new PEPS |Ψ⁡(X0)⟩|\Psi(X_{0})\rangle.

(iv). Repeat steps (ii) and (iii) until the energy EE converges or the gradient stops decreasing. Finally, we regard the output X1X_{1} as an approximate solution of Eq. (4) and |Ψ⁡(X1)⟩|\Psi(X_{1})\rangle as an approximate ground state correspondingly.

It should be noted that, by converting the reduced double-layer structure in Fig. 2(a) to the nested single-layer structure in Fig. 2(c), we have made an acceptable sacrifice to reduce the bond dimension D2D^{2} to D​dDd: the size of the unit cell is doubled from 2×22\times 2 to 4×44\times 4. Therefore, to contract the tensor network by CTMRG, e.g., one has to employ the multisite version of the algorithm adapted to the nested structure. The specific version of the CTMRG algorithm used in this work, for a 4×44\times 4 unit cell, is illustrated in Fig. 3, which is a simple variant of the algorithm proposed in Ref. [14].

Specifically, suppose the distinct tensors in a unit cell are denoted as {T(i,j),i,j=0,1,2,3}\{T^{(i,j)},i,j=0,1,2,3\}, which are all rank-4 tensors with bond dimension DD [44]. In the multisite CTMRG method, the environment of the tensor T(i,j)T^{(i,j)} located at the ii th row and jj th column in the 4×44\times 4 unit cell is represented as {C(i,j,α),E(i,j,β)}\{C^{(i,j;\alpha)},E^{(i,j;\beta)}\}, where α\alpha and β\beta run from 1 to 4 and correspond to the four corner and four edge tensors for each T(i,j)T^{(i,j)}, as illustrated in Fig. 3(a). Therefore, in this case we have 64 distinct corners and 64 edges in total, stored independently for each T(i,j)T^{(i,j)} but updated in a correlated manner. For example, in Fig. 3(b) we explicitly show the recursive relations between the environments of T(i,j)T^{(i,j)} and T(i,j+1)T^{(i,j+1)}, which are used in a left-move step in the CTMRG iterations.

The core step of CTMRG is to find the transformation matrices P(i,j)P^{(i,j)} and Q(i,j)Q^{(i,j)}, which are of dimension D​χD\chi by χ\chi. Here χ\chi is the so-called environment dimension, which is the dimension of the bonds belonging only to the environment tensors. Following the bond density matrix approach developed in Refs. [20, 14], we always use a 2×22\times 2 system surrounded by its environment to determine PP and QQ, as illustrated in Fig. 3(c), where the 4×44\times 4 block is intentionally split into two parts from right. Mathematically, P(i,j)P^{(i,j)} and Q(i+1,j)Q^{(i+1,j)} are constructed in the following

P(i,j)=RstVΛ~−1/2,Q(i+1,j)=RntU∗Λ~−1/2\displaystyle P^{(i,j)}=R_{s}^{t}V\tilde{\Lambda}^{-1/2},\quad Q^{(i+1,j)}=R_{n}^{t}U^{*}\tilde{\Lambda}^{-1/2} (8)

where we have introduced the QR decomposition and singular value decomposition of two matrices NN and SS,

N=Qn​Rn,S=Qs​Rs,Rn​Rst=U​Λ​V†\displaystyle N=Q_{n}R_{n},\quad S=Q_{s}R_{s},\quad R_{n}R_{s}^{t}=U\Lambda V^{\dagger} (9)

Here the superscript tt means matrix transpose. The Λ~\tilde{\Lambda} in Eq. (8) is the truncated version (with dimension χ\chi) of the full singular value matrix Λ\Lambda in Eq. (9). NN is the block tensor with subscripts (a1​a2,a5​a6)(a_{1}a_{2},a_{5}a_{6}) by contracting the eight tensors in the upper part of Fig. 3(c), and SS is tensor with subscripts (a3​a4,a5​a6)(a_{3}a_{4},a_{5}a_{6}) by contracting the lower part. It can be proved that by inserting the transformation matrices P(i,j)​(Q(i+1,j))tP^{(i,j)}\left(Q^{(i+1,j)}\right)^{t} in the bonds labeled by a5​a6a_{5}a_{6} between NN and SS in Fig. 3(c), the resulting network constitutes a truncated singular value decomposition of the bond density matrix ρa1​a2,a3​a4\rho_{a_{1}a_{2},a_{3}a_{4}} which can be expressed as ρ=N​St\rho=NS^{t}.

In a single step of left move, for a 4×44\times 4 unit cell, we need to determine four pairs of transformation matrices by performing Eqs. (8-9) for each ii independently. And after that, one can use these transformations to update the related three environment tensors for each ii by performing the contractions illustrated in Fig. 3(b). This finishes a single step of the left move. We need to perform such a step for each jj, which means we have to perform four such steps in a single left move. Right, upward, and downward moves can be performed one by one similarly, and this completes a single CTMRG iteration. This iteration can be repeated, until all the spectra Λ~\tilde{\Lambda}s converge to some accepted accuracy.

From Fig. 3 and the analysis described above, it is easily shown that if the environment dimension χ\chi is set to the order of D2D^{2} empirically [34], and no symmetry or other advanced techniques like partial matrix decompositions are employed, then the above CTMRG algorithm utilized to contract a nested tensor network with bond dimension DD has a memory cost about D6D^{6} and a computational cost about D9D^{9} [40, 41]. This is more economical than the conventional reduced tensor network method as mentioned in Sec. II.2 and discussed in detail in Ref. [34]. And this is the reason why we can extend our variational calculation equipped with automatic differentiation to D=9D=9 in this work. As also discussed in Ref. [34], as long as χ\chi is sufficiently large, the CTMRG contraction of a nested tensor network (i.e., single-layer) should produce the same result as that of the corresponding reduced tensor network (i.e., double-layer). We verify this by studying the VBS phase of the Shastry-Sutherland model, and the result is shown in the Appendix.

III Results

In this section, we apply the single-layer variational tensor network framework, as explained in the last section, to two prototypical antiferromagnetic quantum spin-1/2 models. Even though neither spin symmetries, such as U(1) and SU(2), nor GPU hardware acceleration are utilized in this work, the ground-state energy and the order parameters characterizing the quantum phases are obtained accurately by pushing D=9D=9. This demonstrates the power of the proposed single-layer framework.

III.1 The Heisenberg model on a square lattice

The first model we studied is the antiferromagnetic spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on a square lattice, which was known to host a Néel antiferromagnetic ground state. To obtain such a state with a double sublattice structure, we use a compatible PEPS ansatz with 2×22\times 2 unit cell containing only two distinct local tensors, as shown in Fig. 4.

The estimated ground-state energy is plotted in Fig. 5 as a function of DD. It shows that the obtained energy systematically decreases as DD increases, verifying the variational nature of the framework. When D=9D=9, we obtain an estimate of Eg=−0.6693896E_{g}=-0.6693896, which is already very close to the value Eg=−0.6694421E_{g}=-0.6694421 in quantum Monte Carlo simulation [35]. If we make a further power-law fitting of Eg​(1/D)E_{g}(1/D), then in the large-DD limit we obtain an extrapolated value of Eg=−0.66941E_{g}=-0.66941, which deviates from the quantum Monte Carlo estimate only by the order of 10−510^{-5}.

As mentioned before, the ground state of this model is antiferromagnetically long-range ordered; therefore, we can use the magnetization MM defined below as an order parameter to characterize the ground state:

M=1N​∑i|mi|,mi=(⟨Sx(i)⟩,⟨Sy(i)⟩,⟨Sz(i)⟩)\displaystyle M=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}|m_{i}|,\quad m_{i}=\left(\langle S^{(i)}_{x}\rangle,\langle S^{(i)}_{y}\rangle,\langle S^{(i)}_{z}\rangle\right) (10)

where Sα(i)S^{(i)}_{\alpha} is the α\alpha component of the spin operator defined on the ii th inequivalent site in the unit cell, |mi||m_{i}| is the length of the magnetic vector mim_{i}, and NN is the total number of inequivalent sites in a unit cell. The obtained magnetization MM as a function of DD is plotted in Fig. 6. Similarly to EgE_{g}, the magnetization is also systematically lowered as DD increases. When D=9D=9, MM is lowered to 0.31897, and the extrapolated value in the large-DD limit obtained by a power fitting of the data M⁡(1/D)M(1/D) gives an estimate M=0.3159M=0.3159, which is only slightly higher than the value M=0.307M=0.307 in quantum Monte Carlo simulation [35], but comparable to those from double-layer and variational update calculations [27, 45]. What is more, we find that the local magnetization mim_{i} exhibits an explicit antiferromagnetic pattern indicated by staggered orientations. All these signatures are consistent with the Néel antiferromagnetic ground state.

As described in Sec. II, there are two important hyperparameters in variational tensor network calculations. One is the bond dimension DD of the PEPS ansatz as expressed in Eq. (), and the other is the environment dimension χ\chi used in the CTMRG algorithms to evaluate ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle for a given DD. Essentially, the calculation is variational with respect to DD, but is not variational for χ\chi. Therefore, for a given DD, the expectation values E⁡(D)E(D) and M⁡(D)M(D) are reliable only under the condition that they are converged with respect to χ\chi as χ\chi increases [34]. Therefore, in this work, in order to ensure the convergence of EE and MM for each DD, we always keep the environment dimension χ\chi sufficiently large. A detailed analysis for D=9D=9 is shown in Fig. 7. It shows that by increasing χ\chi to 160, both the energy and the magnetization are systematically improved, and the convergence error is only of the order of 10−610^{-6}, which is already rather satisfactory for our purpose.

III.2 The frustrated Shastry-Sutherland model

The second model we focused on in this work is the spin-1/2 Shastry-Sutherland model defined by the following Hamiltonian

H=J​∑⟨i,j⟩𝑺i⋅𝑺j+J′​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝑺i⋅𝑺j,J>0,J′>0H=J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\boldsymbol{S}_{i}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{j}+J^{\prime}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\boldsymbol{S}_{i}\cdot\boldsymbol{S}_{j},\quad J>0,\penalty\ J^{\prime}>0 (11)

where 𝑺i\boldsymbol{S}_{i} is the three-component spin operator defined on ii th lattice point. A sketch of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice is illustrated in Fig. 8(a). From the view of the underlying square lattice, one can see that in Eq. (11), JJ denotes the nearest-neighboring antiferromagnetic coupling, and J′J^{\prime} denotes the next-nearest-neighbor coupling defined in only one set of squares and arranged as a wheelchair pattern. This model draws attention in recent years [36, 46, 10, 47] because of the stabilization of a quantum disordered plaquette valence bond solid ground state in the intermediate J/J′J/J^{\prime} regime of the phase diagram, as well as possible realization of a deconfined quantum critical point [48] and/or quantum spin liquid [50, 47, 49] relevant to some interesting experimental results in real materials [51].

An illustration of the phase diagram is also shown in Fig. 8(b). When JJ dominates, the ground state of this model is a Néel antiferromagnetic state, while when J′J^{\prime} dominates, the two spins coupled by J′J^{\prime}, as indicated by the black bonds in Fig. 8(a), form a dimer singlet, and the ground state of the system is a direct product of these dimer singlets. In the intermediate regime, the ground state is a plaquette valence bond solid. However, there is much controversy over the competition between the full-plaquette and empty-plaquette VBS patterns [36, 10, 51], the nature of the phase transition between the Néel and VBS phases [10, 51], and the possible existence of an intervening quantum spin liquid regime [50, 47, 49]. In this work, using the proposed single-layer variational framework and setting J′=1J^{\prime}=1, we focus on two parameter settings: the possible VBS phase with J=0.7J=0.7, and the antiferromagnetic phase with J=0.8J=0.8.

In Fig. 9, we focus on J=0.7J=0.7, and plot the obtained ground-state energy EgE_{g} as a function of DD. The variational feature remains pronounced, i.e., the energy systematically improves as DD becomes larger. When D=9D=9, we have Eg=−0.3880225E_{g}=-0.3880225. If we fit the data Eg​(1/D)E_{g}(1/D) and extrapolate to the large-DD limit, we obtain an estimate Eg=−0.3885E_{g}=-0.3885 [black dashed line in Fig. 9(a)], which is consistent with the previous PEPS from finite systems [47]. To make the result convincing, we analyze the energy for D=9D=9 with χ\chi ranging from 90 to 140 in Fig. 9(b). It is clear that the energy has almost fully converged with a precision of about 10−610^{-6}.

Further analysis shows that the obtained ground state is an empty-plaquette VBS state, which is illustrated in Fig. 8(c). To show this, first we introduce an order parameter MpM_{p} defined as

Mp=14​|∑⟨i,j⟩∈□A⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩−∑⟨i,j⟩∈□B⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩|\displaystyle M_{p}=\frac{1}{4}\Big|\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle\in\square_{A}}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle-\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle\in\square_{B}}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle\Big| (12)

where the two ∑\sum sum over all the nearest-neighbor bond energies in inequivalent empty squares □A\square_{A} and □B\square_{B} [olive and red plaquettes illustrated in Fig. 8(c)]. In Fig. 10(a), we plot the obtained MpM_{p} as a function of DD. It shows clearly that the order parameter converges gradually as DD increases, and when D=9D=9 we obtain Mp=M_{p}= 0.1945. By extrapolating to the large-DD limit, we obtain a final estimate Mp=M_{p}= 0.1930, which is a strong indication that the ground state breaks the Z2Z_{2} symmetry between two inequivalent squares. The convergence with respect to χ\chi plotted in Fig. 10(b) indicates that the symmetry breaking is robust and is not a finite-χ\chi effect. To show the detailed pattern and distinguish the two possible VBS states [10, 36], we plot the bond correlation ⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle for each bond in Fig. 8(c). It shows that the correlation in squares without J′J^{\prime} couplings is much stronger than that in squares with J′J^{\prime} couplings, consistent with the empty-plaquette VBS state. Furthermore, we find the obtained ground state has a tiny magnetization of ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4}, suggesting it probably does not break the SU(2) spin symmetry. Combining these features, we can convincingly conclude that the ground state is an empty-plaquette VBS state at J=0.7J=0.7, consistent with previous studies [10].

For J=0.8J=0.8, we plot the ground-state energy in Fig. 11. The behavior is similar to that for J=0.7J=0.7, and the energy systematically decreases and gradually converges as DD becomes larger. When D=9D=9, we have Eg=−0.448708E_{g}=-0.448708. This is already very close to the previous tensor network studies, such as an infinite projected entangled simplex state (iPESS) study [10], an infinite PEPS study employing U(1) spin symmetry [50], a neural network study [52] and an extrapolation from finite PEPS calculation [47]. These estimate are also included in Fig. 11 for comparison. Extrapolation to the large-DD limit via a simple power-law fitting yields an estimate of Eg=−0.4490E_{g}=-0.4490, which is more reliable. With χ\chi up to 160, Fig. 11 shows that the convergence precision of the ground-state energy for D=9D=9 has reached the order 10−610^{-6}, indicating that the obtained result is convincing.

In Fig. 12, we plot the magnetization MM of the obtained ground state as a function of DD. It shows that though MM becomes weaker and weaker as DD increases, it remains finite and nonzero. For example, when D=9D=9, we still obtain a significant magnetization of about 0.1303, and an extrapolation in the large-DD limit still gives a nonzero estimate of about M=0.12M=0.12. This is neither an artificial finite-χ\chi effect, since by pushing χ\chi to 160, the convergence precision of MM for D=9D=9 has also reached the order 10−610^{-6}, as clearly shown in Fig. 12(b). This is unambiguously consistent with the fact that J=0.8J=0.8 falls in the antiferromagnetic phase.

IV Discussions

In this work, we propose a single-layer framework that integrates the nested tensor network method into the variational tensor network calculations leveraging automatic differentiation. This framework can reduce the memory and computational costs by two and three orders of DD compared to traditional variational calculations, thereby enabling DD to be larger and achieving better accuracy. The validity of the framework is demonstrated through two prototypical models: the square-lattice Heisenberg model and the Shastry-Sutherland model. Even without GPU hardware acceleration or symmetry considerations, we can extend DD to 9, yielding accurate ground-state energies and consistent order parameters with previous studies. In particular, for the Shastry-Sutherland model, we confirm an intermediate empty-plaquette VBS phase in the ground-state phase diagram. The convergence with respect to DD and χ\chi is systematically analyzed, and nearly complete convergence is observed even for the largest DD. We believe this framework could enable large-scale variational tensor network calculations in more complex quantum systems, such as superconductivity [12, 13], excited states, and dynamical studies [53, 11] in the future.

In our calculations, the single-layer tensor network with nested structure is contracted by the CTMRG algorithm. It is known that the idea of nested tensor network can be performed not only in CTMRG [40, 41], but also in other tensor contraction algorithms, such as time-evolving block decimation [34, 42, 43], and coarse-graining renormalization group. Therefore, correspondingly, the single-layer framework in this work can also be realized in other algorithms than CTMRG. The extra acceptable sacrifice is probably the same, i.e., the size of the unit cell of the single-layer nested tensor network may be doubled, as shown in Fig. 2(c) in this work.

The bond dimension DD can be further increased by incorporating additional advanced techniques into this framework. For example, in this work we did not consider the spin symmetry, but one can leverage the U(1) symmetry of the two models to improve efficiency. For the square lattice Heisenberg model in this work, one can utilize a local spin rotation −i​σy-i\sigma_{y} on one set of lattice locations [54, 11] to reduce the 4×44\times 4 unit cell to a 2×22\times 2 unit cell in the generated nested tensor network, which can simplify the calculations shown in Fig. 2(c). Even for the Shastry-Sutherland model, this strategy can accelerate the convergence in variational calculations. Moreover, one can use a checkpoint [27] or a fixed-point technique to reduce the length of the chain, i.e., Eq. (5) used in the back propagation, by calculating the gradient from a given or an approximate fixed-point environment [55]. The latter strategy is similar to the finite-system approximation [56] or to choosing a better initial value for the CTMRG environment and can effectively reduce memory and computational costs in automatic differentiation calculations. Finally, at a purely computational level, one can use partial singular value decomposition, randomized decomposition [57] in Eq. (9), or employ a more economical QR decomposition [58] instead, to reduce computational cost further.

As reviewed in Sec. II.2, the nested tensor network method treats the bra ⟨Ψ|\langle\Psi| and ket |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle independently when contracting ⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle, thus the Hermiticity of the environment (for the reduced tensor) [59] can be easily broken. Fortunately, the Hermiticity can be gradually restored by increasing the environment dimension χ\chi, and could be further improved by considering the hidden Z2Z_{2} symmetry [59], more delicately designed iterations [60], and smarter variation with better convergence [61], etc. The restoration of the Hermiticity is expected to improve the accuracy of the results.

It is worth noting that several recent studies also involve single-layer tensor network states in the literature. For example, in Ref. [60], Jan et al. proposed a similar framework called the split-CTMRG algorithm, which is also based on the nested tensor network structure revealed in Ref. [34]. However, the contraction scheme is particularly designed and differs from what we proposed in Sec. II.3. In Ref. [62], Xu et al. extended the idea of the nested structure to a triple-layer tensor network and applied it to the three-dimensional Ising model successfully, while earlier in Ref. [63], Yang et al. proposed a new nesting structure that is more natural and symmetric than the one proposed in Ref. [34] and was applied successfully to the same model. Probably, these single-layer proposals can be further improved by combining their distinct advantages, which we would like to leave as a future direction.

Appendix

In this appendix, using the Shastry-Sutherland model as an example, we compare results from the single-layer CTMRG and the corresponding double-layer CTMRG. We choose J=0.7J=0.7 (i.e., the plaquette VBS phase), and the wave functions are obtained from the single-layer variational calculations proposed in the main text. The results are plotted in Fig. 13. It shows that for both D=5D=5 and D=8D=8, the single-layer contraction can produce the same results as double-layer contraction as long as χ\chi is sufficiently large (e.g., χ=160\chi=160 in this case). Moreover, at least for this model, the single-layer contraction leads to better convergence. This conclusion is similar to the Kagome Heisenberg model tested in other contraction frameworks [34].
